I farm in Quzhou County, on the North China Plain. The soil here is sandy loam — good for wheat and maize, which is what this land has always grown. The double-cropping calendar is fixed in my bones: winter wheat in October, harvest in June, then summer maize immediately after, harvest in October. I don't deviate from this. The market is reliable, the rotation works well for soil nutrients, and the local grain station buys everything I produce.

My main concern this year, as always, is water. The aquifer under Quzhou has been dropping for thirty years. I've read the provincial reports. I keep my irrigation at three applications for wheat — no more — and I rely on summer rainfall to carry the maize most of the way. I've switched to rotary tillage for wheat and no-tillage for maize to lock moisture in.

I grow hybrid seed for maize — Zhengdan 958, proven yield. For wheat, I use Jimai 22, which has good resistance to stripe rust and performs well under our conditions. I apply nitrogen in two splits for wheat to reduce losses. My fertilizer rates are slightly below the county average because I've seen that over-application past a threshold doesn't pay back in yield.

I keep about 2 mu for vegetables — mainly garlic and spinach interplanted — for household use and the local wet market. Not worth including in the formal plan.
